summary.text: Factoring each binomial quotient into its multiples-of-p and p-unit parts, then pairing k with p^r-k, gives the common expansion \(R_c=1+c(c+1)p^{2r}T\pmod {p^{3r+3}}\); reciprocal power-sum identities show that \(T\) is divisible by \(p^r\) for \(p\ge5\) and by \(3^{r-1}\) for \(p=3\), while the quadratic remainder vanishes. Substitution makes the desired difference a multiple of \(T(2\binom{3p^{r-1}}{p^{r-1}}^2-9\binom{2p^{r-1}}{p^{r-1}})\) plus a multiple of \(T^2\), and the bracket is divisible by \(p^3\) (respectively \(3^4\)), using stabilization of the lower binomial coefficients modulo that power and a direct base computation for \(p=3\), so both terms have the required valuation.

full_proof.text:
Let
\[
a(n)=\binom{3n}{n}^{2}-27\binom{2n}{n}.
\]
Fix a prime \(p\ge 3\) and an integer \(r\ge2\). Put
\[
q=p^r,\qquad m=p^{r-1},\qquad K=3r+3.
\]
We prove that \(a(q)=a(m)\) in \(\mathbb Z/p^K\mathbb Z\). All inverses below are taken in an indicated ring \(\mathbb Z/p^e\mathbb Z\); every integer being inverted is prime to \(p\), so these inverses exist.

For an integer \(Q\) divisible by \(p\), write
\[
U_p(Q)=\{k:1\le k\le Q,\ p\nmid k\},
\qquad
L_p(Q)=\{k\in U_p(Q):k\le Q/2\}.
\]
Since \(p\) and hence \(Q=p^s\) are odd, reflection \(k\mapsto Q-k\) is a bijection from \(L_p(Q)\) onto the other half of \(U_p(Q)\).

We begin with a binomial-product identity. For every \(c,Q\ge0\),
\[
\binom{(c+1)Q}{Q}\prod_{k=1}^{Q}k
 =\prod_{k=1}^{Q}(cQ+k).                                      \tag{1}
\]
Suppose that \(Q=pn\). Separate in both products the terms whose indices are multiples of \(p\). The denominator terms with such indices are \(pj\), \(1\le j\le n\), and the corresponding numerator terms are
\[
cQ+pj=p(cn+j).
\]
After cancelling the common product of the factors \(p\), and then using (1) with \(n\) in place of \(Q\), one obtains
\[
\binom{(c+1)pn}{pn}\prod_{k\in U_p(pn)}k
 =\binom{(c+1)n}{n}\prod_{k\in U_p(pn)}(cpn+k).                \tag{2}
\]
Consequently, modulo any power \(p^e\),
\[
\binom{(c+1)pn}{pn}
 =\binom{(c+1)n}{n}R_c(pn),                                   \tag{3}
\]
where
\[
R_c(Q)=\prod_{k\in U_p(Q)}\frac{cQ+k}{k}.
\]
Indeed, the product of all the \(k\in U_p(Q)\) is a unit modulo \(p^e\), so it may be cancelled in (2).

We next analyze \(R_c(Q)\), for \(Q=p^s\). Pair the factor indexed by \(k\in L_p(Q)\) with that indexed by \(Q-k\). If
\[
t_k=\frac1{k(Q-k)},
\]
then a direct calculation gives
\[
\begin{aligned}
\frac{cQ+k}{k}\frac{cQ+(Q-k)}{Q-k}
 &=\left(1+\frac{cQ}{k}\right)
   \left(1+\frac{cQ}{Q-k}\right)\\
 &=1+cQ\left(\frac1k+\frac1{Q-k}\right)
      +\frac{c^2Q^2}{k(Q-k)}\\
 &=1+c(c+1)Q^2t_k.                                             \tag{4}
\end{aligned}
\]
Here we used
\[
\frac1k+\frac1{Q-k}=\frac{Q}{k(Q-k)}.
\]
Thus
\[
R_c(Q)=\prod_{k\in L_p(Q)}(1+A t_k),
\qquad A=c(c+1)Q^2.                                           \tag{5}
\]
Define
\[
T_p(Q)=\sum_{k\in L_p(Q)}t_k,
\qquad
E_p(Q)=\sum_{\substack{\{i,j\}\subset L_p(Q)\\i\ne j}}t_it_j,
\]
where the second sum is over unordered two-element subsets. Expanding (5), if \(A^3=0\) in the ring under consideration, gives
\[
R_c(Q)=1+A T_p(Q)+A^2E_p(Q).                                  \tag{6}
\]
All terms involving at least three distinct \(t_k\)'s contain \(A^3\) and vanish.

We need divisibility information about \(T_p(Q)\) and \(E_p(Q)\). First we prove the stronger estimates for \(T_p(Q)\).

Let
\[
S(N)=\sum_{k=1}^{N}k^2=\frac{N(N+1)(2N+1)}6
\]
and
\[
V_p(Q)=\sum_{k\in U_p(Q)}k^2.
\]
Separating multiples of \(p\) gives
\[
S(pn)=p^2S(n)+V_p(pn).                                       \tag{7}
\]
If \(N\) is coprime to \(6\), the displayed formula for \(S(N)\) shows that \(N\mid S(N)\): because \(N\) is coprime to \(6\), one may cancel \(6\) from the divisibility \(N\mid6S(N)\). Hence, if \(p\ge5\) and \(Q=p^s=pn\), both \(n\) and \(Q\) are coprime to \(6\). Thus \(Q\mid S(Q)\), and \(n\mid S(n)\), which implies \(Q=pn\mid p^2S(n)\). Equation (7) therefore yields
\[
Q\mid V_p(Q) \qquad (p\ge5).                                \tag{8}
\]

For \(p=3\), let \(Q=3^s\) with \(s\ge1\). We claim
\[
3^{s-1}\mid V_3(3^s).                                        \tag{9}
\]
Write \(Q=3n\), where \(n=3^{s-1}\). More generally, if an odd integer \(N\) is divisible by \(3\), then
\[
N/3\mid S(N).
\]
Indeed, from \(6S(N)=N(N+1)(2N+1)\), division by \(3\) gives
\[
2S(N)=(N/3)(N+1)(2N+1),
\]
and \(N/3\) is odd, so it is coprime to \(2\) and can be cancelled. Applying this first to \(3n\) gives \(n\mid S(3n)\). Also \(n\mid9S(n)\): this is immediate when \(n=1\), while for \(n>1\) the same argument gives \(n/3\mid S(n)\), and therefore certainly \(n\mid9S(n)\). Now (7), with \(p=3\), shows that \(n\mid V_3(3n)\), proving (9).

We relate these square sums to \(T_p(Q)\). Work first modulo \(Q=p^s\). Reflection gives
\[
2T_p(Q)=\sum_{k\in U_p(Q)}\frac1{k(Q-k)}.
\]
Since \(Q-k\equiv-k\pmod Q\),
\[
\frac1{k(Q-k)}\equiv-\frac1{k^2}\pmod Q.
\]
Inversion permutes the reduced residue classes modulo \(Q\). Therefore
\[
\sum_{k\in U_p(Q)}\frac1{k^2}
 \equiv\sum_{k\in U_p(Q)}k^2=V_p(Q)\pmod Q,
\]
and hence
\[
2T_p(Q)\equiv-V_p(Q)\pmod Q.                                \tag{10}
\]
Because \(p\) is odd, \(2\) is invertible modulo every power of \(p\). It follows from (8) and (10) that, for \(p\ge5\),
\[
T_p(p^s)\equiv0\pmod{p^s}.                                  \tag{11}
\]
For \(p=3\), (9) and the same argument, reduced modulo \(3^{s-1}\), give
\[
T_3(3^s)\equiv0\pmod{3^{s-1}}.                              \tag{12}
\]
These statements remain valid when the sums are regarded modulo a larger power of \(p\): reduction to the stated smaller modulus commutes with all the inverses, and an element reducing to zero modulo \(p^d\) is a multiple of \(p^d\) in the larger residue ring.

We also need
\[
E_p(p^s)\equiv0\pmod p\qquad(s\ge2).                        \tag{13}
\]
To prove it, first note that for every positive integer \(d\),
\[
\sum_{k\in U_p(p^s)}k^{-d}\equiv0\pmod p\qquad(s\ge2).      \tag{14}
\]
Indeed, modulo \(p\) the summand is periodic with period \(p\), while the interval of length \(p^s\) consists of \(p^{s-1}\) such periods. The multiplier \(p^{s-1}\) is zero modulo \(p\). Multiples of \(p\) contribute nothing if one extends the summand by zero there.

Modulo \(p\), we have \(t_k\equiv-k^{-2}\). Reflection again shows that the full sum over \(U_p(p^s)\) is twice the sum over \(L_p(p^s)\). Using (14) with \(d=2\), and cancelling \(2\), gives
\[
\sum_{k\in L_p(p^s)}t_k=0\pmod p.
\]
Similarly, using \(d=4\),
\[
\sum_{k\in L_p(p^s)}t_k^2=0\pmod p.
\]
Finally,
\[
\left(\sum_k t_k\right)^2=\sum_k t_k^2+2E_p(p^s).
\]
The first two terms vanish modulo \(p\), and \(2\) is invertible, proving (13).

We can now obtain the ratio expansion needed at level \(Q=q=p^r\), modulo \(p^K\). In (5), \(A=c(c+1)q^2\). Since
\[
A^3\text{ is divisible by }q^6=p^{6r},
\]
and \(6r\ge3r+3=K\) for \(r\ge1\), we have \(A^3=0\pmod{p^K}\). Thus (6) applies. By (13), \(E_p(q)\) contains a factor \(p\), so
\[
A^2E_p(q)
\]
is divisible by \(q^4p=p^{4r+1}\). For \(r\ge2\), \(4r+1\ge3r+3\), and this term also vanishes modulo \(p^K\). Therefore
\[
R_c(q)\equiv1+c(c+1)q^2T_p(q)\pmod{p^K}.                    \tag{15}
\]

We next establish the small-modulus binomial congruences that will provide an extra factor in the final cancellation.

Suppose first that \(p\ge5\). We claim that for every \(s\ge0\),
\[
\binom{(c+1)p^s}{p^s}\equiv c+1\pmod{p^3}.                  \tag{16}
\]
It suffices, by (3), to show \(R_c(p^s)\equiv1\pmod{p^3}\) for \(s\ge1\). In (5), \(A=c(c+1)p^{2s}\). Every term of degree at least two in \(A\) is divisible by \(p^{4s}\), hence by \(p^3\). If \(s=1\), (11) supplies one further factor \(p\) in the linear term \(AT_p(p)\), so that it is divisible by \(p^3\). If \(s\ge2\), \(A\) itself is divisible by \(p^4\). Thus the ratio is \(1\) modulo \(p^3\). Iterating (3) down from \(p^s\) to \(1\), where \(\binom{c+1}{1}=c+1\), proves (16).

For \(p=3\), the corresponding statement is that for every \(s\ge1\),
\[
\binom{(c+1)3^s}{3^s}\equiv\binom{3(c+1)}3\pmod{3^4}.       \tag{17}
\]
For every step with \(s\ge2\), (5) and (12) show that \(R_c(3^s)\equiv1\pmod{3^4}\). Indeed, terms of degree at least two contain \(3^{4s}\), and the linear term contains \(3^{2s}\cdot3^{s-1}=3^{3s-1}\), whose exponent is at least \(5\). Iterating (3) down to exponent \(1\) proves (17).

Return to \(m=p^{r-1}\), and set
\[
C=\binom{3m}{m},\qquad B=\binom{2m}{m}.
\]
For \(p\ge5\), (16), with \(c=2\) and \(c=1\), gives
\[
C\equiv3\pmod{p^3},\qquad B\equiv2\pmod{p^3}.
\]
Consequently
\[
2C^2-9B\equiv2\cdot3^2-9\cdot2=0\pmod{p^3}.                \tag{18}
\]
For \(p=3\), (17) gives
\[
C\equiv\binom93=84\pmod{3^4},
\qquad
B\equiv\binom63=20\pmod{3^4}.
\]
The required explicit calculation is
\[
2\cdot84^2-9\cdot20=13932=81\cdot172.
\]
Thus
\[
2C^2-9B\equiv0\pmod{3^4}.                                  \tag{19}
\]

We now complete the proof. Work modulo \(p^K\), and abbreviate
\[
T=T_p(q),\qquad X=q^2T.
\]
Applying (3) with \(n=m\), and then (15), gives
\[
\binom{3q}{q}=C\,R_2(q)\equiv C(1+6X)\pmod{p^K},             \tag{20}
\]
and
\[
\binom{2q}{q}=B\,R_1(q)\equiv B(1+2X)\pmod{p^K}.             \tag{21}
\]
Substitution into \(a(q)\), followed by an elementary expansion, yields
\[
\begin{aligned}
a(q)-a(m)
&\equiv [C(1+6X)]^2-27B(1+2X)-(C^2-27B)\\
&=6X(2C^2-9B)+36C^2X^2.                                     \tag{22}
\end{aligned}
\]

There are two cases.

If \(p\ge5\), (11) says that \(T\) is divisible by \(q=p^r\). Hence
\[
X=q^2T\quad\text{is divisible by }p^{3r}.
\]
By (18), \(2C^2-9B\) is divisible by \(p^3\). Therefore the first term on the right of (22) is divisible by \(p^{3r+3}=p^K\). Also \(X^2\) is divisible by \(p^{6r}\), and \(6r\ge3r+3\), so the second term is divisible by \(p^K\).

If \(p=3\), (12) says that \(T\) is divisible by \(3^{r-1}\). Therefore
\[
X=q^2T\quad\text{is divisible by }3^{2r+r-1}=3^{3r-1}.
\]
By (19), \(2C^2-9B\) is divisible by \(3^4\). Thus the first term in (22) is divisible by
\[
3^{(3r-1)+4}=3^{3r+3}=3^K.
\]
The square \(X^2\) is divisible by \(3^{6r-2}\), and for \(r\ge2\),
\[
6r-2\ge3r+3.
\]
Hence the second term in (22) is also divisible by \(3^K\).

In either case, (22) gives
\[
a(p^r)-a(p^{r-1})\equiv0\pmod{p^{3r+3}}.
\]
Equivalently,
\[
\boxed{a(p^r)\equiv a(p^{r-1})\pmod{p^{3r+3}}},
\]
as required.
